arXiv:2604.14993v1 [cs.DC] 16 Apr 2026

Serving Chain-structured Jobs with Large Memory Footprints with Application to Large Foundation Model Serving

Tingyang Sun Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University Email: tfs5679@psu.edu    Ting He Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University Email: tinghe@psu.edu    I-Hong Hou Affiliation: Texas A&M University Email: ihou@tamu.edu
Abstract

As a current trend in Artificial Intelligence (AI), large foundation models are increasingly employed as the core of AI services. However, even after training, serving such models at scale remains a challenging task due to their heavy resource footprints, particularly in terms of GPU memory. While recent works revealed unique characteristics of systems serving foundation models that distinguish them from traditional distributed computing systems, there is still a lack of fundamental understanding of the underlying system management problems. This work aims at addressing this gap by extracting a novel problem of “server chain composition” via block placement and cache allocation for serving chain-structured jobs with large memory footprints, which models a fundamental problem in serving large foundation models through pipeline parallelism. After showing the NP-hardness of the optimal solution, the focus is turned to developing scalable algorithms with guaranteed performance under state-of-the-art load balancing. Application of the proposed solution to a distributed large language model (LLM) serving system shows significant reduction of response times compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

1 Introduction

Widely regarded as one of the most promising approaches towards realizing Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), large foundation models such as large language models (LLMs), large vision models, and related multimodal models are gaining popularity in both research communities and industries. The widespread deployment of such models introduces a system-level question of how to efficiently host these models and use them to answer queries (i.e., inference requests) at scale, given limited GPU resources. Due to the large sizes of foundation models and the high cost of high-end GPUs, model parallelism, where a model is split across multiple GPUs/GPU servers, becomes a popular model serving approach. In particular, for physically distributed servers, the dominant approach is to split the model at the boundary of layers, a.k.a. pipeline parallelism, which essentially places each model instance onto a chain of servers that are invoked sequentially during inference.

Serving large foundation models is fundamentally different from serving traditional workloads. Most foundation models are based on the transformer architecture, including all the LLMs (e.g., GPT series, LLaMA), vision foundation models such as Vision Transformer (ViT), and the backbone of most multimodal models (e.g., GPT-4V, Gemini). A large transformer has a massive memory footprint for storing both the model parameters (i.e., tensor weights) and the intermediate values generated during inference (i.e., KV values of the past tokens). This memory-intensive nature makes GPU memory the bottleneck resource in serving such models, which leads to fundamentally different resource allocation problems from serving traditional compute-bound workloads.

In this work, we tackle a fundamental resource allocation problem underlying the emerging application of pipeline-parallel processing of inference requests by transformer-based large models. Abstracting a given model as a chain of blocks (e.g., each representing a transformer layer) and the inference requests as jobs, we focus on the composition of server chains by strategically placing the blocks onto servers and allocating cache space at each server for storing the intermediate values during job processing, to optimize the system performance in combination with a state-of-the-art load balancing policy. We further provide explicit performance bounds to not only characterize the performance of the resulting system but also guide the tuning of an important design parameter therein.

1.1 Related Work

Model-parallel model serving: One line of related works is on distributed serving of large models, a.k.a. model-parallel model serving. This includes pipeline parallelism that splits the model at the granularity of layers [12, 22, 35], and tensor parallelism that splits the model at the granularity of neurons [16, 4, 30]. Tensor parallelism incurs a higher communication overhead across the splits and is thus typically limited within a single multi-GPU server [31]. In contrast, pipeline parallelism only requires communications between adjacent splits and is thus more suitable for distributed settings. There are a few systems that support model-parallel model serving with focus on LLMs, such as vLLM with Ray Serve [1], Nvidia Dynamo [23], Amazon EKS [3], and PETALS [6]. Except for PETALS, most of these systems are designed for highly-connected environments (e.g., datacenters), while PETALS can work on weakly-connected devices. Most of the existing efforts focused on system implementation and ignored the fundamental problems in managing such systems, which is the gap addressed by this work. Such problems only started to receive attention recently, where [29] considered a problem formulated after PETALS [6] called “block placement and request scheduling”. However, the solution therein contained many implementation-specific artifacts and was heuristic in nature. In this work, we will deepen this investigation by abstracting the fundamental problems in managing large model serving systems from a job processing perspective and developing scalable solutions as well as performance analysis.

Service function chaining: Another line of related works is on service function chaining (SFC) [19]. Under pipeline parallelism, each inference request is served by a chain of servers, which makes the resource allocation problem resemble the problem of service function (SF) placement and flow routing in the context of SFC [19]. SFC placement and routing has been studied in the networking community, with domain-specific objectives (e.g., minimizing network operation cost or maximizing flow rate) [7] and mostly heuristic solutions [14, 7] (except for a few special cases such as [36, 10, 28]). Despite the conceptual similarity, SFC is fundamentally different from pipeline-parallel model serving: (i) difference SFs have heterogeneous resource requirements [14, 36, 13] and some SFs may change the flow rate [18] or branch an input flow into multiple output flows [13], while transformer layers of the same transformer model are typically identically-structured modules with the same resource requirements and input/output data size; (ii) more importantly, the bottleneck resource in large model serving is typically GPU memory, which differs from the bottleneck resource in SFC --- compute cycles --- in how it is consumed by the workloads11 1 The part of GPU memory used to store model parameters is shared by all the processed requests while the part used to store KV values for each request is dedicated to this request, differing from the additive consumption of compute cycles [36, 10]..

Load balancing: Viewing each inference request as a job, our problem can be viewed as a job processing problem where the processing is distributed to a chain of servers. In a multi-server context, most existing works focused on load balancing with given servers, including Join-the-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) [34], Join-the-Idle-Queue (JIQ) [17], and their low-overhead alternatives (e.g., JSQ-dd [21] and JIQ-dd [32]) for homogeneous servers, and later adaptations like Speed-Aware JSQ (SA-JSQ) [5] (a.k.a. Join-the-Fastest-of-the-Shortest-Queue (JFSQ) [33]) for heterogeneous servers. However, in our case, a major challenge is how to “compose the servers” by distributing model parameters and allocating KV caches, as serving an inference request not only requires a chain of servers hosting all the model parameters but also enough cache space at each server for the intermediate values. A related problem of job scheduling in LLM serving was discussed in [20], which considered scheduling inference requests to a single LLM instance; in our case, the deployed blocks may form many (partially overlapping) model instances and the solutions in [20] can be used for scheduling within each instance after dispatching. A seemingly related problem is “job shop scheduling” [9], where each job has a chain of operations to be performed sequentially by a set of machines and each machine can only perform one operation at a time. However, our problem differs not only in that our machine-operation association is controllable (through block placement), but also in that in our case the operations of the same job need to be scheduled simultaneously instead of sequentially22 2 This is because although microscopically the forward pass in generating each token is processed sequentially by the layers, macroscopically the inference session for serving each request needs to be run simultaneously at all the servers in the selected server chain to perform sequence generation in an auto-regressive manner.. To our knowledge, the problem of processing chain-structured memory-bound jobs by composable server chains has not been formally studied before.

1.2 Summary of Contributions

We tackle a novel problem of processing chain-structured memory-bound jobs by composable server chains, inspired by pipeline-parallel processing of inference requests for large transformer models, with the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We decompose the resource allocation problem in such a system into three coupled subproblems, targeting at optimizing (i) the placement of service blocks across servers to form server chains, (ii) the allocation of cache space at each server to determine the (concurrency) capacity of each server chain, and (iii) the dispatching of jobs to the server chains. The first two subproblems are solved offline to compose “job servers” that can each serve a job independently, and the third is solved online to load balance among the “job servers”.

  2. 2.

    The main difficulty resides in the first two subproblems, both of which are NP-hard and contend for the limited server memory. Under a state-of-the-art load balancing policy of “Join-the-Fastest-Free-Server”, we develop a set of efficient algorithms for the first two subproblems that achieve optimality in important special cases, and provide explicit analysis in terms of upper/lower bounds on the steady-state mean response time.

  3. 3.

    We test our proposed solution against state-of-the-art resource allocation algorithms for distributed LLM serving via both model-driven simulations and experiments based on a real LLM serving system. Besides validating our theoretical analysis, these tests also show that the proposed solution can provide significant performance improvement (with 6363–77%77\% reduction in mean response time) under real demands deviating from our original assumptions, which indicates the robustness of our solution.

Roadmap. Section 2 presents our problem formulation, Section 3 describes the proposed solution and its analysis, Section 4 tests the proposed solution against benchmarks in serving LLM inference requests, and Section 5 concludes the paper with a discussion. All the proofs are provided in Appendix A.2.

2 Problem Formulation

2.1 System Model

2.1.1 Abstract Model

Consider a system consisting of a set 𝒥\mathcal{J} of J:=|𝒥|J:=|\mathcal{J}| servers. Each server j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} has a memory size of MjM_{j} and incurs a mean communication time of τjc\tau^{c}_{j} to participate in a job’s processing and a mean computation time of τjp\tau^{p}_{j} to process each service block for the job.

The system hosts a service consisting of LL blocks, each with block size sms_{m}, to serve dynamically arriving jobs. When serving a job, a server needs to cache the intermediate results from each block it processes for the job, with a cache size of scs_{c} per block per job. To be successfully served, a job needs to (i) be assigned to a chain of servers that collectively host all the LL blocks in order and (ii) be allocated enough cache space at each server. Due to the communication overhead, we consider block placements that place a continuous range of blocks at each server, represented by {aj,…,aj+mj−1}\{a_{j},\ldots,a_{j}+m_{j}-1\} for server j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, where aja_{j} denotes the index of the first block and mjm_{j} the number of blocks, and thus the entire block placement can be represented by (𝒂:=(aj)j∈𝒥,𝒎:=(mj)j∈𝒥)(\bm{a}:=(a_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{J}},\>\bm{m}:=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{J}}). 2.1.2 Connection to Large Model Serving

The above system model is inspired by systems used to serve inference requests for transformer-based large models through pipeline parallelism, where the service represents a large transformer with decoder-only architecture that is used by many state-of-the-art large foundation models (e.g., GPTs).

Specifically, each “job” represents an inference request that aims at generating a sequence of output tokens based on a sequence of input tokens, where most of the processing is carried out in a set of identically structured transformer layers. Each “service block” represents such a transformer layer, and each “cache” represents a KV cache used to store the context information in the form of KV values of the past tokens (including input tokens) processed for a given request by a given transformer layer. Serving a job includes both a prefill phase, which populates the caches with KV values from processing the input tokens, and a decode phase, which generates the output tokens one by one by passing the latest token through the transformer layers auto-regressively. We assume static cache allocation, which pre-allocates a fixed-size cache for each transformer layer at the beginning of each job processing according to a predetermined maximum sequence length. We assume that once a job starts its processing at a chain of servers, it must run there until completion (i.e., no migration or preemption), which holds in most practical systems due to the high overhead in transferring/swapping KV caches. The mean communication time τjc\tau^{c}_{j} represents the mean total time for communicating the input/output to server jj in generating all the tokens for a request44 4 This model fits the communication method in PETALS [6] with a frontend server as the proxy of clients, where the frontend server connects the servers in a chain by sending the input to a server and then forwarding its output to the next server. Our solution can be adapted to the case where consecutively traversed servers directly communicate as in [1], by making the communication time dependent on the preceding server, i.e., τi​jc\tau^{c}_{ij}, and taking τjc:=maxi⁡τi​jc\tau^{c}_{j}:=\max_{i}\tau^{c}_{ij}., and the mean per-block computation time τjp\tau^{p}_{j} represents the mean total time in processing all the tokens for a request by a transformer layer.

While this system model omits some possible complications55 5 For example, the KV cache size can vary across requests and even grow during the processing of the same request if dynamic allocation is used., it captures the main difference between serving inference requests for large transformers and traditional workloads: the shift of bottleneck resource from compute/network to memory, induced by the large memory footprints of transformers, the relatively small runtime bandwidth demands, and the massive parallel processing capabilities of GPUs. This shift leads to a novel challenge in resource allocation: as (GPU) memory is a critical resource for both placing blocks and processing inference requests (due to the need of KV caches), there is a resource contention between the model placement stage and the request serving stage, as the residual memory after model placement determines how many requests each server can process in parallel. We will address this contention explicitly.

2.2 Optimization Problems

Our overall goal is to optimize the system’s performance by strategically composing server chains and using the composed chains to process incoming jobs. In this work, we assume a centralized orchestrator that controls these decisions and serves as the ingress/egress point of jobs; distributed variations are left to future work. We focus on services with a large memory footprint (e.g., large foundation models), where loading service blocks to servers takes substantial time. This motivates us to consider a two-time-scale approach: server chain composition via block placement and cache allocation at a large time scale, and load balancing for assigning incoming jobs to the composed server chains at a small time scale.

Offline Server Chain Composition: As mentioned in Section 1.1, one of the main differences between our problem and classical job serving problems is that the “job servers” in our case, each representing a chain of servers with resources for serving a job independently, are composable. Their composition depends on not only how the blocks are placed onto the physical servers, but also how each server allocates its residual memory among the server chains traversing it as caches for ongoing jobs.

Specifically, since under a given block placement (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}), each ongoing job traversing (i,j)∈ℰ𝒂,𝒎(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}} (i.e., processed by servers ii and jj consecutively) consumes mi​jm_{ij} cache slots at server jj (each of size scs_{c}), we can represent the cache allocation by a vector 𝒄:=(ck)k∈𝒦𝒂,𝒎\bm{c}:=(c_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}} that specifies the maximum number of jobs processed concurrently on all the feasible server chains. We refer to ckc_{k} as the capacity of chain kk. Then mi​j​ckm_{ij}c_{k} is the number of cache slots server jj allocates to a chain kk that traverses it from server ii. According to the memory consumption model (1), the cache allocation 𝒄\bm{c} must satisfy

∑i:(i,j)∈ℰ𝒂,𝒎mi​j∑k:(i,j)∈kck≤⌊Mj−sm​mjsc⌋=:M~j,∀j∈𝒥,\displaystyle\sum_{i:\>(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}}m_{ij}\sum_{k:\>(i,j)\in k}c_{k}\leq\left\lfloor{M_{j}-s_{m}m_{j}\over s_{c}}\right\rfloor=:\widetilde{M}_{j},~~~\forall j\in\mathcal{J}, (3)

where M~j\widetilde{M}_{j} denotes the number of cache slots at server jj after hosting mjm_{j} blocks.

From a job processing perspective, each feasible server chain kk with capacity ckc_{k} can process up to kk jobs in parallel (with possibly different processing times), we model such a server chain as ckc_{k} “virtual servers” that can each serve one job at a time in the queueing-theoretic sense. We refer to such virtual servers as job servers to differentiate from the physical servers. Let μk:=1/Tk\mu_{k}:=1/T_{k} denote the service rate of chain kk, where TkT_{k} is the mean service time defined in (2). Then the block placement (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}) determines the set of feasible server chains 𝒦𝒂,𝒎\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}} and their service rates (μk)k∈𝒦𝒂,𝒎(\mu_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}}, while the cache allocation determines the capacity of each chain (ck)k∈𝒦𝒂,𝒎(c_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}}. Together, they compose a set of job servers (μk,ck)k∈𝒦𝒂,𝒎(\mu_{k},c_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}}, where there are ckc_{k} job servers of service rate μk\mu_{k}.

Online Load Balancing: Given the job servers composed by block placement and cache allocation, the remaining problem reduces to a classical online load balancing problem where the orchestrator dispatches incoming jobs to the composed job servers, which are generally heterogeneous in terms of service rates. This suggests that we can borrow from the existing solutions on load balancing for heterogeneous servers such as [33, 5]. A subtle difference in our case is that the job servers are logical servers instead of physical servers, and thus any arrived job will be kept in a central queue by the orchestrator before processing. Although any work-conserving load balancing policy can stabilize the system for arrival rates within the total service rate, defined as

ν:=∑k∈𝒦𝒂,𝒎μk​ck,\displaystyle\nu:=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}}\mu_{k}c_{k}, (4)

different policies can lead to different response times.

Design Objective: Given a request arrival rate λ\lambda, our goal is to jointly design the block placement, the cache allocation, and the load balancing policy so as to minimize the mean response time (including waiting and processing), while ensuring queue stability.

Remark: In this work, we assume the standard First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS) scheduling to focus on the above optimizations. Our solution can be combined with optimizations of job scheduling as in [20] for further improvement, which is left to future work.

3 Optimized Job Serving

We now address the optimization problems identified in Section 2.2, with focus on developing scalable algorithms.

3.1 Server Chain Composition

3.1.1 Optimization Formulation

As explained in Section 2.2, the block placement (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}) and the cache allocation 𝒄\bm{c} jointly determine the feasible server chains and their capacities, which provides the job servers for subsequent processing. Since the ultimate performance depends on how jobs are assigned to the composed job servers, ideally we should design (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}) and 𝒄\bm{c} with the load balancing policy in mind. 3.1.2 NP-hardness

The optimization (7) is a complex integer programming problem with nonlinear constraints. Moreover, the number of variables in 𝒄\bm{c} scales with the number of feasible chains |𝒦𝒂,𝒎||\mathcal{K}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}|, which is generally exponential in the size of the system. Rigorously, we can prove that even though the block placement is given, the remaining cache allocation problem is still NP-hard.

Theorem 3.1.

Computing the optimal cache allocation as in (7) is NP-hard even if the server chains are given.

Remark: Theorem 3.1 implies that even if the block placement is given, optimizing server chain composition remains a hard problem.

3.1.3 Block Placement

Intuitively, block placement depends on the cache allocation strategy as the latter defines how the placed blocks will be used to form job servers. Since the cache allocation subproblem is already NP-hard by Theorem 3.1, we need a simpler (but possibly suboptimal) cache allocation strategy to facilitate the optimization of block placement. In particular, the proof of Theorem 3.1 implies that the cause of the hardness of cache allocation is the sharing of servers across chains. This inspires us to restrict our solution space to disjoint server chains that can each host the entire set of blocks with sufficient capacity.

Simplification: Given a required capacity c∈ℤ+c\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} denoting the minimum number of jobs each server needs to serve concurrently, the maximum number of blocks we can place at server jj is

mj​(c):=min⁡(⌊Mjsm+sc​c⌋,L),\displaystyle m_{j}(c):=\min\left(\left\lfloor{M_{j}\over s_{m}+s_{c}c}\right\rfloor,\>L\right), (8)

obtained by reserving cc cache slots for each placed block. Accordingly, the mean service time each job spends at this server is upper-bounded by

tj​(c):=τjc+τjp​mj​(c),\displaystyle t_{j}(c):=\tau^{c}_{j}+\tau^{p}_{j}m_{j}(c), (9)

achieved when all the mj​(c)m_{j}(c) blocks are processed. For now we treat cc as a given parameter, which will be optimized later (see (14)).

Forming disjoint server chains is equivalent to selecting disjoint subsets of servers such that each subset has enough memory to host all the blocks. Under cache allocation according to a required capacity cc, the resulting total service rate can be bounded as follows.

Lemma 3.2.

Given a collection of disjoint subsets of servers (𝒥k)k∈𝒦(\mathcal{J}_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}} such that ∑j∈𝒥kmj​(c)≥L\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}m_{j}(c)\geq L for all k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}, the block placement that places the entire set of LL blocks onto each subset 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} with mj​(c)m_{j}(c) blocks at each server j∈𝒥kj\in\mathcal{J}_{k} can achieve a total service rate of no less than c​∑k∈𝒦(∑j∈𝒥ktj​(c))−1c\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}t_{j}(c))^{-1}.

By restricting the solution space to disjoint server chains and reserving cache space according to the required capacity, we can simplify the joint optimization problem in (7) as follows:

min(𝒥k)k∈𝒦\displaystyle\min_{(\mathcal{J}_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}}}\quad |𝒦|\displaystyle|\mathcal{K}| (10a)
s.t. ∑k∈𝒦1∑j∈𝒥ktj​(c)≥λρ¯​c,\displaystyle\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}t_{j}(c)}\geq{\lambda\over\overline{\rho}c}, (10b)
∑j∈𝒥kmj​(c)≥L,∀k∈𝒦,\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}m_{j}(c)\geq L,~~~\forall k\in\mathcal{K}, (10c)
𝒥k∩𝒥k′=∅,∀k,k′∈𝒦,k≠k′,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{k}\cap\mathcal{J}_{k^{\prime}}=\emptyset,~~~\forall k,k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K},\>k\neq k^{\prime}, (10d)
𝒥k⊆𝒥,∀k∈𝒦,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{J},~~~\forall k\in\mathcal{K}, (10e)

which aims at grouping the servers into the smallest number of disjoint subsets (ensured by (10d)–(10e)), subject to constraint (10c) that ensures each subset to form a feasible server chain of capacity cc, and constraint (10b) that ensures a sufficiently large total service rate according to Lemma 3.2.

Algorithm: The simplified problem in (10) is still NP-hard.

Lemma 3.3.

The optimization in (10) is NP-hard.

Nevertheless, this simplified problem formulation inspires an intuitive block placement algorithm. The basic intuition is that “chaining fast servers together is better than mixing fast and slow servers”. For example, if ∃\existstwo subsets of servers 𝒥1,𝒥2\mathcal{J}_{1},\mathcal{J}_{2} not satisfying (10c) yet with ∑j∈𝒥1tj​(c)<∑j∈𝒥2tj​(c)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}t_{j}(c)<\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}t_{j}(c), and two servers j1,j2j_{1},j_{2} not in either subset that satisfy mji​(c)≥max⁡(L−∑j∈𝒥1mj​(c),L−∑j∈𝒥2mj​(c))m_{j_{i}}(c)\geq\max(L-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}m_{j}(c),\>L-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}m_{j}(c)) (i=1,2i=1,2) and tj1​(c)<tj2​(c)t_{j_{1}}(c)<t_{j_{2}}(c), then one can verify that

1∑j∈𝒥1tj​(c)+tj1​(c)+1∑j∈𝒥2tj​(c)+tj2​(c)>\displaystyle{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}t_{j}(c)+t_{j_{1}}(c)}+{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}t_{j}(c)+t_{j_{2}}(c)}>
1∑j∈𝒥1tj​(c)+tj2​(c)+1∑j∈𝒥2tj​(c)+tj1​(c).\displaystyle\hskip 60.00009pt{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}t_{j}(c)+t_{j_{2}}(c)}+{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}t_{j}(c)+t_{j_{1}}(c)}. (11)

Thus, we can always achieve a higher total service rate by a given number of chains by adding a faster server to a faster chain and a slower server to a slower chain. Since different servers can host different numbers of blocks, we compare server speeds by the amortized mean service time per block, given by

t~j​(c):=tj​(c)mj​(c).\displaystyle\widetilde{t}_{j}(c):={t_{j}(c)\over m_{j}(c)}. (12)

These ideas lead to a greedy block placement algorithm referred to as Greedy Block Placement with Cache Reservation (GBP-CR), shown in Alg. 1, which sequentially places blocks onto servers in descending speeds to form server chains (lines 1–1), until all the servers are processed or the scaled total service rate (denoted by ν\nu) satisfies the given requirement (line 1).

Complexity: Alg. 1 has a near-linear time complexity of O⁡(J​log⁡J)O(J\log{J}), dominated by the sorting of servers in line 1.

Analysis: As an efficient solution, GBP-CR is expected to be generally suboptimal for (10) due to the NP-hardness of the problem. Nevertheless, GBP-CR is optimal in a special case of practical relevance. Specifically, consider the case where all the servers have an identical memory size Mj≡MM_{j}\equiv M (∀j∈𝒥\forall j\in\mathcal{J}). This can be caused by servers having a standard memory configuration (e.g., 8 GB for consumer GPUs or 80 GB for datacenter GPUs) or owners limiting the amount of memory made available to the model serving system even if the servers may have more physical memory (e.g., when the GPUs are contributed by volunteers as in the case of PETALS [6]). In this special case, GBP-CR is optimal in the following sense.

Theorem 3.4.

In the case of homogeneous memory, i.e., Mj≡MM_{j}\equiv M (∀j∈𝒥\forall j\in\mathcal{J}), GBP-CR (Alg. 1) provides an optimal solution to (10).

Parameter tuning: The performance of GBP-CR (Alg. 1) crucially depends on its input parameter cc, which controls a “service time vs. waiting time” tradeoff: a smaller cc allows more blocks to be placed at each server, which helps to shorten server chains and thus reduce service times; meanwhile, a larger cc leaves the servers with more residual memory after block placement, which allows them to run more jobs concurrently that helps to reduce waiting times.

To illustrate this tradeoff, consider the example in Fig. 1, where the squares denote blocks and the circles denote servers. Under c=1c=1, we have mj​(c)≡Lm_{j}(c)\equiv L, which leads to LL single-server chains as shown in Fig. 1a, each of capacity 11. This configuration yields a mean service time of T(1)=τc+L​τpT^{(1)}=\tau^{c}+L\tau^{p} and a total service rate of ν(1)=L/(τc+L​τp)\nu^{(1)}=L/(\tau^{c}+L\tau^{p}). Under c=L2c=L^{2}, we have mj​(c)≡1m_{j}(c)\equiv 1, which leads to a single LL-server chain as shown in Fig. 1b with capacity L2L^{2}. This configuration yields a mean service time of T(2)=L​τc+L​τpT^{(2)}=L\tau^{c}+L\tau^{p} and a total service rate of ν(2)=L/(τc+τp)\nu^{(2)}=L/(\tau^{c}+\tau^{p}). We see that T(1)<T(2)T^{(1)}<T^{(2)} but ν(2)>ν(1)\nu^{(2)}>\nu^{(1)}, i.e., the second configuration is more suitable for high demands and the first configuration is more suitable for low demands. This indicates the existence of a demand-dependent optimal configuration of cc.

Let cmax:=⌊(maxj⁡Mj−sm)/sc⌋c_{\max}:=\lfloor(\max_{j}M_{j}-s_{m})/s_{c}\rfloor denote the maximum number of concurrent jobs supported by any server. Assuming GBP-CR as the block placement algorithm, we can measure the performance under a given configuration of cc by the objective value of (10) achieved by GBP-CR for a required capacity of cc, given by

K⁡(c):=min⁡{K:∑l=1K1∑j∈kl​(c)tj​(c)≥λρ¯​c},\displaystyle K(c):=\min\{K:\>\sum_{l=1}^{K}{1\over\sum_{j\in k_{l}(c)}t_{j}(c)}\geq{\lambda\over\overline{\rho}c}\}, (13)

where kl​(c)k_{l}(c) denotes the ll-th server chain constructed by GBP-CR under capacity cc. Then the optimal configuration is given by

c∗:=arg⁡minc∈[cmax]⁡c⋅K⁡(c).\displaystyle c^{*}:=\argmin_{c\in[c_{\max}]}c\cdot K(c). (14)

By the argument in Section 3.1.1, such a configuration will minimize a surrogate of the mean response time if the jobs are processed by the disjoint server chains constructed by GBP-CR with a given capacity. The optimization (14) is easy to solve via brute-force search due to its small 1D solution space.

3.1.4 Cache Allocation

Although during block placement, GBP-CR already reserves cache space at each server for processing cc jobs concurrently, the residual memory often allows more concurrency via proper cache allocation.

Example: Consider the problem instance in Fig. 2, where the amortized mean service time for server jlj_{l} (l∈[5]l\in[5]) under c=1c=1 is t~jl​(c)=1+l​ϵ\widetilde{t}_{j_{l}}(c)=1+l\epsilon. GBP-CR will form two disjoint server chains k1=j1→j2k_{1}=j_{1}\to j_{2} and k2=j3→j4→j5k_{2}=j_{3}\to j_{4}\to j_{5} as shown in Fig. 2a, each with a capacity of c=1c=1, which yields a total service rate of

ν=13+5​ϵ+13+12​ϵ.\displaystyle\nu={1\over 3+5\epsilon}+{1\over 3+12\epsilon}. (15)

Meanwhile, any directed path traversing all the 3 blocks is a feasible server chain as shown in Fig. 2b, and the residual memory allows us to simultaneously run c1=5c_{1}=5 jobs on chain k1k_{1}, c2=5c_{2}=5 jobs on chain k2k_{2}, and c3=5c_{3}=5 jobs on a new chain k3=j1→j4→j5k_{3}=j_{1}\to j_{4}\to j_{5}, achieving a higher total service rate of

ν=53+5​ϵ+53+10​ϵ+53+12​ϵ\displaystyle\nu={5\over 3+5\epsilon}+{5\over 3+10\epsilon}+{5\over 3+12\epsilon} (16)

under the same block placement. This example suggests the need to further optimize server chain composition after block placement.

Algorithm: The main challenge is complexity. In addition to the NP-hardness of optimal cache allocation as stated in Theorem 3.1, the dimension of the solution space is also large. Specifically, let 𝒢𝒂,𝒎=(𝒥+,ℰ𝒂,𝒎)\mathcal{G}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}=(\mathcal{J}_{+},\mathcal{E}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}) denote a logical routing topology under a given block placement (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}), formed by the extended server set 𝒥+\mathcal{J}_{+} and the set ℰ𝒂,𝒎\mathcal{E}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}} of server pairs that can be traversed consecutively. Then each path in 𝒢𝒂,𝒎\mathcal{G}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}} from the dummy server j0j_{0} to the dummy server jJ+1j_{J+1} represents a valid server chain that traverses all the blocks in order, as illustrated by Fig. 2b. Generally, the number of possible server chains under a given block placement is exponential in the number of servers, which causes severe challenges for cache allocation. Fortunately, a given load balancing policy may only assign jobs to a subset of all the possible server chains, which allows efficient cache allocation by only focusing on this subset.

In particular, for load balancing among heterogeneous job servers with a central queue as considered in this work, a state-of-the-art load balancing policy is Join-the-Fastest-Free-Server (JFFS) [5]. Under JFFS, each incoming job will either be assigned to the fastest free job server if there is any, or entered into a central queue if none of the job servers is free. We find that this policy only utilizes a polynomial-sized subset of possible server chains, identified by Greedy Cache Allocation (GCA) as shown in Alg. 2. Let Mj(l)M^{(l)}_{j} denote the residual memory at server jj after constructing and allocating cache for ll chains, measured in the number of cache slots; initially, Mj(0)=M~jM^{(0)}_{j}=\widetilde{M}_{j} as defined in (3). Recall from Section 2.1 that mi​j:=aj+mj−ai−mim_{ij}:=a_{j}+m_{j}-a_{i}-m_{i} is the number of cache slots occupied at server jj by each job processed by servers ii and jj consecutively. The algorithm sequentially allocates cache space by (i) finding the fastest chain among all the possible chains with available memory for at least one more job using shortest path routing (line 2), (ii) allocating as much cache space as possible to this chain to maximize the number of jobs it can process concurrently (line 2), and (iii) updating the residual server memory (line 2) as well as the server pairs that can serve at least one more job concurrently (lines 2–2). The process continues until no more job can be served using the remaining server memory. For example, for the block placement in Fig. 2b, GCA constructs 33 server chains 𝒦={j1→j2,j1→j4→j5,j3→j4→j5}\mathcal{K}=\{j_{1}\to j_{2},j_{1}\to j_{4}\to j_{5},j_{3}\to j_{4}\to j_{5}\} with a capacity of 55 each.

Complexity: Each while loop in Alg. 2 will remove at least one link, as the link (i∗,j∗)∈kl(i^{*},j^{*})\in k_{l} achieving the min\min in line 2 must have Mj∗(l)<mi∗​j∗M^{(l)}_{j^{*}}<m_{i^{*}j^{*}} and thus be removed in line 2. Thus, the number of while loops is bounded by O⁡(|ℰ(0)|)=O⁡(J2)O(|\mathcal{E}^{(0)}|)=O(J^{2}). The time for each while loop is dominated by the time for shortest path routing in line 2, which is O⁡(J​log⁡J+J2)O(J\log{J}+J^{2}). Thus, the total time complexity of Alg. 2 is bounded by O⁡(J4)O(J^{4}). This analysis also implies that the number of server chains constructed by GCA is bounded by O⁡(J2)O(J^{2}), which can be much smaller than the total number of possible chains under the given block placement.

Analysis: Even if the server chains constructed by GCA only constitute a small subset of all possible chains, they are sufficient for supporting JFFS type of job assignment as proved below.

Theorem 3.5.

Under any given block placement (𝒂,𝒎)(\bm{a},\bm{m}), if GCA (Alg. 2) returns a set of server chains 𝒦\mathcal{K} and the corresponding capacities (ck)k∈𝒦(c_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}}, then to assign jobs according to the principle of JFFS, it suffices to limit the utilized server chains to 𝒦\mathcal{K} and the number of concurrent jobs on each chain k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K} to ckc_{k}.

Remark: Theorem 3.5 implies that instead of considering all the exponentially many possible server chains, we only need to consider the O⁡(J2)O(J^{2}) server chains constructed by GCA and bound their capacities accordingly, if the load balancing policy is JFFS. Note that this holds under any block placement, not only the block placement given by GBP-CR.

3.2 Load Balancing

As explained in Section 2.2, after server chain composition (via block placement and cache allocation), the remaining task for the orchestrator becomes a classical load balancing problem of assigning incoming jobs to the composed server chains under their capacity constraints. In particular, since our system has a central queue, we can apply the JFFS policy [5], which has demonstrated superior empirical performance in comparison to the state-of-the-art load balancing policies with dedicated queues [2] and been used to establish a lower bound on mean response time for stationary load balancing policies [5].

3.2.1 Adaptation of JFFS

Since the original JFFS does not consider parallel processing at servers, we need to adapt it to account for the capability for a server chain to process multiple jobs in parallel. The adapted policy is shown in Alg. 3, referred to as Join-the-Fastest-Free-Chain (JFFC). Here Zk​(t)Z_{k}(t) (k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}) denotes the number of ongoing jobs on chain kk, and Q⁡(t)Q(t) denotes the number of jobs waiting in the central queue, both at time tt.

3.2.2 Response Time Analysis

Our focus is on the steady-state mean response time. For this analysis, we assume that:

  1. 1.

    Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ\lambda, each requiring an independent and exponentially distributed amount of work with mean 11 (i.e., the service times for a server chain with service rate μ\mu are independent and exponentially distributed with mean 1/μ1/\mu);

  2. 2.

    The service times are independent of the inter-arrival times.

We note that Poisson arrivals and exponential service times are standard assumptions for steady-state analysis of load balancing systems and not needed in our previous algorithm development or analysis. As shown later (Section 4.2), while real arrival processes and service times may deviate from these assumptions, analytical results derived from these assumptions still provide meaningful guidance in practice.

For the ease of presentation, we sort the server chains into descending order of service rates {kl}l∈[K]\{k_{l}\}_{l\in[K]} (K:=|𝒦|K:=|\mathcal{K}|), and use μl\mu_{l}/clc_{l} to denote the service rate/capacity of the ll-th fastest chain klk_{l}. We denote the system state at time tt by a vector 𝒁⁡(t)\bm{Z}(t), where Z0​(t)Z_{0}(t) is the number of queued jobs and Zl​(t)Z_{l}(t) (l∈[K]l\in[K]) is the number of ongoing jobs on the ll-th fastest chain. Under the above assumptions, (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} is a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC), with a state space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} consisting of two disjoint parts:

𝒵1\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}_{1} :={𝒛:z0=0 and zl∈{0,…,cl},∀l∈[K]},\displaystyle:=\{\bm{z}:\>z_{0}=0\mbox{ and }z_{l}\in\{0,\ldots,c_{l}\},\forall l\in[K]\}, (17)
𝒵2\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}_{2} :={(n,c1,…,cK):n∈ℤ+}.\displaystyle:=\{(n,c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}):\>n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}\}. (18)

Under JFFC, the transition rate from 𝒛\bm{z} to 𝒛′\bm{z}^{\prime} is given by77 7 We use 𝒙i1:i2\bm{x}_{i_{1}:i_{2}} to denote the vector (xi)i=i1i2(x_{i})_{i=i_{1}}^{i_{2}} of a sub-range of elements.

q(𝒛,𝒛′)={λif ​𝒛​ transitions into ​𝒛′​ upon an arrival,zl​μlif z′0=z0=0,z′l=zl−1,z′l′=zl′(∀l′≠l),∑l=1Kcl​μlif z′0=z0−1,𝒛′1:K=𝒛1:K=𝒄1:K,0o.w.,\displaystyle\hskip-7.5ptq(\bm{z},\bm{z}^{\prime})\hskip-2.5pt=\hskip-2.5pt\left\{\hskip-5.0pt\begin{array}[]{ll}\lambda&\hskip-20.00003pt\mbox{if }\bm{z}\mbox{ transitions into }\bm{z}^{\prime}\mbox{ upon an arrival},\\ z_{l}\mu_{l}&\hskip-20.00003pt\mbox{if }z^{\prime}_{0}=z_{0}=0,z^{\prime}_{l}=z_{l}-1,z^{\prime}_{l^{\prime}}=z_{l^{\prime}}(\forall l^{\prime}\neq l),\\ \sum_{l=1}^{K}c_{l}\mu_{l}&\mbox{if }z^{\prime}_{0}=z_{0}-1,\bm{z}^{\prime}_{1:K}=\bm{z}_{1:K}=\bm{c}_{1:K},\\ 0&\mbox{o.w.,}\end{array}\right.

where 𝒛\bm{z} upon an arrival will transition into 𝒛′\bm{z}^{\prime} with z0′=z0+1z^{\prime}_{0}=z_{0}+1 and 𝒛′1:K=𝒛1:K\bm{z}^{\prime}_{1:K}=\bm{z}_{1:K} if 𝒛1:K=𝒄1:K\bm{z}_{1:K}=\bm{c}_{1:K} (i.e., all the chains are fully occupied), or zl∗′=zl∗+1z^{\prime}_{l^{*}}=z_{l^{*}}+1 if ∃l∗=arg⁡min⁡{l:zl<cl}\exists l^{*}=\argmin\{l:\>z_{l}<c_{l}\} and zl′=zlz^{\prime}_{l}=z_{l} for l≠l∗l\neq l^{*} (i.e., kl∗k_{l^{*}} is the fastest chain with available capacity).

JFFC is throughput-optimal, i.e., it guarantees stability whenever the arrival rate is less than the total service rate, as stated below.

Lemma 3.6.

The CTMC (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} with transition rate (3.2.2) is ergodic for any λ<∑l=1Kcl​μl\lambda<\sum_{l=1}^{K}c_{l}\mu_{l}.

Lemma 3.6 implies that as long as λ<∑l=1Kcl​μl\lambda<\sum_{l=1}^{K}c_{l}\mu_{l}, the system will have a unique steady-state distribution, denoted by 𝛑\bm{\pi}, which characterizes the steady-state mean response time T¯\overline{T} by Little’s law as

T¯=𝔼𝝅​[∑l=0KZl]/λ,\displaystyle\overline{T}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\pi}}\left[\sum_{l=0}^{K}Z_{l}\right]/\lambda, (23)

where 𝒁∼𝝅\bm{Z}\sim\bm{\pi} is the steady-state system state. Exact analysis of the steady-state distribution of (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} is highly challenging due to the high-dimensional nature of the state space; see Appendix A.3 for the exact analysis in a special case of K=2K=2. Nevertheless, by collapsing the states with suitably defined transition rates, we can derive closed-form upper/lower bounds as follows.

Define 𝒵n:={𝒛∈𝒵:∑l=0Kzl=n}\mathcal{Z}_{n}:=\{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}:\>\sum_{l=0}^{K}z_{l}=n\} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) as the subset of states with nn jobs in the system. Then in the steady state, the flow balance equation between 𝒵n−1\mathcal{Z}_{n-1} and 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n} is given by

λ​∑𝒛∈𝒵n−1π𝒛=∑𝒛∈𝒵nπ𝒛​(∑l=1Kzl​μl)=νn​∑𝒛∈𝒵nπ𝒛,\displaystyle\lambda\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n-1}}\pi_{\bm{z}}=\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\pi_{\bm{z}}\left(\sum_{l=1}^{K}z_{l}\mu_{l}\right)=\nu_{n}\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\pi_{\bm{z}}, (24)

where νn\nu_{n} is the average steady-state death rate for 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}_{n}, defined as

νn:=∑𝒛∈𝒵nπ𝒛∑𝒛′∈𝒵nπ𝒛′​∑l=1Kzl​μl.\displaystyle\nu_{n}:=\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}{\pi_{\bm{z}}\over\sum_{\bm{z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\pi_{\bm{z}^{\prime}}}\sum_{l=1}^{K}z_{l}\mu_{l}. (25)

Therefore, if (νn)n∈ℕ(\nu_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is known, we can construct a birth-death process with a scalar state Φ⁡(t)\Phi(t) that represents the total number of jobs in the system at time tt, with a fixed birth rate λ\lambda and a state-dependent death rate νn\nu_{n} for each n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The steady-state distribution ϕ\bm{\phi} of this process must satisfy the flow balance equation λ​ϕn−1=νn​ϕn\lambda\phi_{n-1}=\nu_{n}\phi_{n}, which compared to (24) implies ϕn=∑𝒛∈𝒵nπ𝒛\phi_{n}=\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\pi_{\bm{z}}, i.e.,

𝔼𝝅​[∑l=0KZl]=∑n=0∞n​∑𝒛∈𝒵nπ𝒛=∑n=0∞n​ϕn=𝔼ϕ​[Φ].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\pi}}\left[\sum_{l=0}^{K}Z_{l}\right]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n}}\pi_{\bm{z}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\phi_{n}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\phi}}[\Phi]. (26)

Thus, (Φ⁡(t))t≥0(\Phi(t))_{t\geq 0} is equivalent to (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} in terms of mean system occupancy and hence mean response time in the steady state.

However, we cannot construct (Φ⁡(t))t≥0(\Phi(t))_{t\geq 0} as we do not know the death rate νn\nu_{n} that depends on the unknown steady state distribution of (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} through (25). Nevertheless, we can bound νn\nu_{n} by88 8 We use (x)+(x)_{+} to denote max⁡(x, 0)\max(x,\>0).

Their steady-state distributions help to bound the steady-state mean occupancy of our system as follows.

Plugging the bounds from Theorem 3.7 into (23) then yields closed-form upper and lower bounds on the steady-state mean response time under JFFC.

Remark: We note that the existing analysis of JFFS in [5] only modeled the system state by a scalar Z⁡(t):=∑l=0KZl​(t)Z(t):=\sum_{l=0}^{K}Z_{l}(t) (i.e., the total number of jobs in the system at time tt), under the assumption that jobs will always occupy the fastest job servers under JFFS. In contrast, we show that this assumption is incorrect in the steady state (see the example in Appendix A.3), and only leads to a lower bound as shown by Theorem 3.7.

3.2.3 Improved Parameter Tuning

The closed-form bounds in Theorem 3.7 enable another method of tuning parameter cc in GBP-CR (Alg. 1): instead of minimizing the surrogate objective in (14), we can choose cc to minimize the upper/lower bound in Theorem 3.7 for the chains constructed by GBP-CR (Alg. 1) and GCA (Alg. 2). Compared to the surrogate objective, these bounds better represent the actual mean response time under the proposed solution, which leads to better parameter tuning (see Fig. 6), at the cost of slightly more computation at the orchestrator (because instead of only running GBP-CR for each candidate value of cc, the orchestrator now needs to run both GBP-CR and GCA).

4 Performance Evaluation

We will test our proposed solutions against benchmarks in serving LLM inference requests by distributed GPU nodes via two complementary evaluation methods: (i) model-driven simulations that validate our solution under its original assumptions, and (ii) experiments that evaluate the actual performance when applying our solution to a leading open-source Internet‑distributed LLM inference system called PETALS [6].

4.1 Model-driven Simulations

4.1.1 Simulation Settings

We simulate the processing of chain-structured jobs according to the system model in Section 2.1, with parameters set to represent the use case of pipeline-parallel LLM inference99 9 Our simulation code is available at: https://github.com/TingyangSunJeff/load_balance_llm_simulator.. Specifically, we set sm=1.32s_{m}=1.32 GB and sc=0.11s_{c}=0.11 GB according to the tensor sizes for model parameters and KV cache1010 10 The KV cache size is computed based on a maximum sequence length of 2048. per transformer layer and L=70L=70 according to the number of layers for BLOOM-176B [26]. Assuming an average input length of 2,0002,000 tokens and an average output length of 2020 tokens according to the traces from [24], we set MjM_{j} and τjp\tau^{p}_{j} according to two types of GPUs: Mj=40M_{j}=40 GB and τjp=109\tau^{p}_{j}=109 ms1111 11 Let to≈1t_{o}\approx 1 ms denote the per-block overhead time, tjIt^{I}_{j} denote the per-block-per-token prefill time, tjOt^{O}_{j} denote the per-block-per-token decode time, and l¯i​n\overline{l}_{in}/l¯o​u​t\overline{l}_{out} denote the average input/output length. Then τjp=to+tjI​l¯i​n+tjO​(l¯o​u​t−1)\tau^{p}_{j}=t_{o}+t^{I}_{j}\overline{l}_{in}+t^{O}_{j}(\overline{l}_{out}-1). BLOOM-176B requires F=5F=5 GFLOPs per block per token and sm=1.32s_{m}=1.32 GB per block under NF4, which means that for a server with fjf_{j} TFLOPS and bjb_{j} GB/ms memory bandwidth, tjI≈F/fjt^{I}_{j}\approx F/f_{j} ms and tjO≈sm/bjt^{O}_{j}\approx s_{m}/b_{j} ms, as prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound. for a high-performance GPU node with 120 TFLOPS and a memory bandwidth of 1.021.02 GB/ms, and Mj=20M_{j}=20 GB and τjp=175\tau^{p}_{j}=175 ms for a low-performance GPU node with 80 TFLOPS and a memory bandwidth of 0.510.51 GB/ms. These GPU types are comparable to slices of A100 (3g.40gb and 2g.20gb) generated by Nvidia’s multi-instance GPU technology [8].

We consider geographically-distributed deployments as targeted by PETALS [6], and set τjc\tau^{c}_{j} according to the communication delays in a real wide-area network, the RIPE Atlas European network [25]. To simulate the communication method in PETALS [6], where the node initiating an inference session (i.e., the orchestrator) relays data between servers, we set τjc\tau^{c}_{j} according to the RTT between the nodes hosting the orchestrator and server jj, plus 1818 ms to account for overhead (e.g., serialization or deserialization time). We randomly select one node as the orchestrator location and JJ other nodes as server locations, where η\eta fraction of randomly selected servers are equipped with high-performance GPUs and the rest are equipped with low-performance GPUs. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process of rate λ\lambda, each having an independent and exponentially distributed size with mean 11, where serving a job of size rr by a server chain with service rate μk\mu_{k} takes time r/μkr/\mu_{k}. By default, J=20J=20, η=0.2\eta=0.2, λ=0.2​requests/s\lambda=0.2~\text{requests/s}, and ρ¯=0.7\overline{\rho}=0.7. Results are averaged over 20 Monte Carlo runs.

4.1.2 Unit Tests

We first validate the performance of individual algorithms under their design assumptions.

Block placement: To evaluate GBP-CR (Alg. 1) in solving (10), we compare the objective in (10a) scaled by cc, which is a surrogate for the mean response time, between GBP-CR and 100100 randomly generated feasible block placements reported as a box–whisker plot in Fig. 3. To validate Theorem 3.4 (optimality of GBP-CR under homogeneous memory), we separately test a homogeneous case (Fig. 3(a)) and a heterogeneous case (Fig. 3(b)). In both cases, GBP-CR achieves equally good or better performance compared to the best solution found by randomized brute-force search.

Cache allocation: To evaluate GCA (Alg. 2) in solving (7) under a given block placement, we assess the number of “job servers” to achieve a required total service rate of λ/ρ¯\lambda/\overline{\rho} as in (7a) (the smaller, the better). Under a block placement given by GBP-CR, we compare the performance of GCA with (i) an upper bound yielded by only using the disjoint server chains and the reserved cache space given by GBP-CR (‘c⋅K⁡(c)c\cdot K(c)’); (ii) a lower bound given by ⌈λ/(ρ¯​μ1)⌉\lceil\lambda/(\overline{\rho}\mu_{1})\rceil, where μ1\mu_{1} is the highest service rate per chain (‘Lower Bound’); (iii) a conditionally optimal cache allocation by solving the integer linear program resulting from plugging the server chains constructed by GCA into (7) (‘Optimal ILP’). The result in Fig. 4 shows that further optimizing cache allocation by GCA can substantially improve the performance and even achieve optimality under light loads.

Load balancing: We evaluate JFFC (Alg. 3) under a fixed set of server chains and their capacities given by GBP-CR + GCA in terms of the mean response time. Fig. 5(a) shows the comparison with other load balancing policies, including baselines like Join-the-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) [34] and Joint-the-Idle-Queue (JIQ) [17] as well as more advanced policies like Smallest-Expected-Delay (SED) and Speed-Aware JSQ (SA-JSQ) [5] (all the policies have been extended to account for parallel processing). Fig. 5(b) shows the comparison with the lower/upper bound from Theorem 3.7. The results not only validate the state-of-the-art performance of JFFC, but also illustrate the gap between its actual performance and the bound that has been ignored in [5]. Moreover, we also observe that a large percentage (over 85%85\%) of the mean response time for JFFC is the mean service time when the load factor is below 0.70.7, which justifies our selection of ρ¯\overline{\rho}.

Parameter tuning: Fig. 6 shows the impact of the design parameter cc in GBP-CR, which controls cache reservation, on the mean response time. In addition to the actual mean response time from simulations, we also evaluate: (i) the value of c⋅K⁡(c)/λc\cdot K(c)/\lambda that represents the objective of (14) (where dividing by λ\lambda converts its meaning to time) and (ii) the upper/lower bound from Theorem 3.7. All the curves demonstrate a significant impact of cc, which is not monotone. For example, the value of c⋅K⁡(c)/λc\cdot K(c)/\lambda grows linearly with cc most of the time, but when cc increases beyond a threshold, the number of disjoint chains K⁡(c)K(c) will decrease by one due to having fewer blocks per server, which will cause c⋅K⁡(c)/λc\cdot K(c)/\lambda to decrease by roughly c/λc/\lambda. While the objective of (14) leads to too little cache reservation and the upper bound from Theorem 3.7 leads to too much cache reservation, the lower bound from Theorem 3.7 yields a configuration c∗c^{*} that minimizes the mean response time by reserving the right amount of cache space for each placed block.

Fig. 7 further evaluates how the optimal c∗c^{*} varies with the arrival rate λ\lambda. The lower bound from Theorem 3.7 exhibits a monotone trend: at low arrival rates, it suggests smaller c∗c^{*} values, resulting in more memory being allocated to block placement to form shorter server chains and minimize service times; as the arrival rate increases, its suggested c∗c^{*} increases to allocate more memory to caches, enabling higher parallelism to handle the increased load. While simulation results show some variance due to randomness in the request process, they generally align with the lower bound’s suggestion, validating its effectiveness for parameter tuning across different demand levels. In contrast, the c∗c^{*} value derived from the upper bound in Theorem 3.7 is overly aggressive and the c∗c^{*} value derived from the surrogate objective c⋅K⁡(c)/λc\cdot K(c)/\lambda is overly conservative.

4.1.3 Overall Comparison

We compare the overall performance in terms of mean response time of the proposed solution, GBP-CR (for c=7c=7) + GCA + JFFC, against two state-of-the-art solutions:

  • •

    ‘PETALS’: the current resource allocation algorithms used in the PETALS system [6], which greedily place blocks and route inference requests according to heuristic metrics;

  • •

    ‘BPRR’: a recently proposed solution from [29], which employs a two-time-scale algorithm to place blocks and dynamically route requests without explicitly composing server chains or allocating cache space ahead of time.

The results in Fig. 8 under various server configurations show that: (i) by explicitly optimizing the composition of server chains, the proposed solution can significantly improve the performance over the state of the art (with 8% – 83% reduction in mean response time), and (ii) the improvement is more prominent in more resource-constrained environments with fewer servers (smaller JJ) or a smaller fraction of high-performance servers (smaller η\eta).

4.2 PETALS-based Experiments

4.2.1 Experiment Settings

We modify PETALS [6] to implement the proposed server chain composition and load balancing algorithms1212 12 The modified PETALS code is available at: https://github.com/TingyangSunJeff/petals_llm_chain_scheduling.. We deploy the system onto a server with 3 A100 (80 GB) GPUs, where we leverage the multi-instance GPU technology [8] to partition each A100 into 2 lower-performance GPUs (2g.20gb) and 1 higher-performance GPU (3g.40gb) that together emulate 9 servers with one GPU each. Due to the limited GPUs, we use a smaller model LLaMA-2-7B for the experiment. We use the namespace and the traffic control features of Linux [27] to simulate network latency according to the RTTs in RIPE Atlas European network [25] as described in Section 4.1.1. We generate requests according to the Azure LLM inference trace from [24], which contains the arrival times and the numbers of input/output tokens from sampled LLM inference services in Azure, collected on November 11th 2023. The trace has an average rate of 2.572.57 requests/s, an average input length of 2048 tokens, and an average output length of 28 tokens.

4.2.2 Model Validation

We start by estimating the parameters in our system model (e.g., τjp\tau^{p}_{j}, τjc\tau^{c}_{j}) and validating the resulting model with measurements from our PETALS deployment. Fig. 9 shows the computation time at a given server, decomposed into prefill time and decode time (of all generated tokens), as a function of the number of processed blocks, the output length, and the input length. The results validate that the overall computation time grows linearly with the number of processed blocks as assumed in (2). Moreover, the decode time grows linearly with the output length and the prefill time grows linearly with the input length, as assumed in footnote 11. Fig. 10 shows the communication time in invoking a given server, decomposed into communication time in generating the first token (during prefill) and communication time in generating the remaining tokens (during decode). This time is independent of the GPU type or the number of blocks processed at the server. The post-first-token communication time is strongly dependent on the output length due to autoregressive decoding. The first-token communication time weakly depends on the input length (due to data transfer time). In all cases, our system model closely matches the actual measurement.

We then test the assumptions of Poisson arrivals and exponentially distributed service times used in our mean response time analysis (Section 3.2.2) against measurements based on the trace. The results in Fig. 11 indicate that the actual distributions notably deviate from our theoretical assumptions: (i) the inter-arrival times are more bursty than exponential distribution with the same mean (the std ratio between the actual and the exponential distributions is 13.15), while (ii) the service times are less bursty than exponential distribution with the same mean (the std ratios is 0.71–0.81). Nevertheless, our proposed solution configured under these simplifying assumptions remains highly effective as shown below.

4.2.3 Performance Comparison

We compare the response times between the proposed solution and the benchmarks described in Section 4.1.3. The results, given in Table 1, show substantial performance difference for different resource allocation algorithms, where BPRR [29] reduces the mean response time by 36.9%36.9\% compared to the current algorithms used in PETALS [6], and the proposed solution increases such reduction to 76.8%76.8\% (a 63.1%63.1\% reduction compared to BPRR). A closer look at the response time components shows that most of the improvement comes from reducing the waiting times, while the service times remain similar. Note that although the model used in this experiment is small enough to fit in an individual server, the high arrival rate in the trace leads to a large amount of cache reservation (c=35c=35 according to the lower bound in Theorem 3.7), which causes the model to be split across multiple servers1313 13 LLaMA-2-7B has 32 transformer blocks. Under c=35c=35, each 3g.40gb can only hold 24 blocks and each 2g.20gb can only hold 12 blocks.. To test the efficacy of our cache reservation strategy, we further evaluate a benchmark that places an entire model instance onto each server and uses JFFC for load balancing. The results (‘JFFC only’ in Table 1) demonstrate an intermediate response time performance between the proposed solution and the benchmarks from [6, 29]. Closer examination shows that compared to the proposed solution, placing the entire model onto each server leads to less cache space at inference time, which reduces the parallel job-processing capability of faster servers that forces more requests to be assigned to slower servers (which increases service times) or queued (which increases waiting times). Moreover, requiring a single server to process all the blocks also increases the cache requirement for each active job that leads to lower memory utilization. In our experiment, the KV cache requirement on a server processing all the blocks is ∼2\sim 2 GiB per active inference session. In this case, a server at its concurrency limit can still have free-but-unusable memory of up to 22 GiB, which amounts to 10%10\% of the HBM on 2g.20gb and 5%5\% on 3g.40gb.

5 Conclusion

We have addressed a resource allocation problem in serving chain-structured jobs with large memory footprints by composable server chains, inspired by pipeline-parallel processing of inference requests for large transformers. Based on the unique requirements of such workloads, we formulate and solve a set of novel optimizations aimed at optimally composing server chains to minimize the mean response time. Our experiments based on a real LLM serving system and real demand traces show that the proposed solution is highly effective in reducing the response time compared to state-of-the-art solutions. Meanwhile, fully optimizing large model serving involves many other considerations, such as time-varying demands and additional control knobs allowed by modern model serving systems. Our optimization-based approach has laid a solid foundation for addressing these problems in future research.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Notation

Table 2 summarizes the main notation used in this paper, where the first half are input parameters and the second half are decision variables (including both independent and dependent variables).

A.2 Supporting Proofs

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

We prove the conclusion by reducing the Multidimensional Knapsack Problem (MKP) to an instance of our problem. According to [15], the MKP has the following form:

max𝒄\displaystyle\max_{\bm{c}}\quad ∑k=1Kμk​ck\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{k}c_{k} (32a)
s.t. ∑k=1Kmj​k​ck≤Dj,∀j∈[d],\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{jk}c_{k}\leq D_{j},~~~\forall j\in[d], (32b)
ck∈{0,1},∀k∈[K],\displaystyle c_{k}\in\{0,1\},~~~\forall k\in[K], (32c)

which tries to select from a given set of KK dd-dimensional items, each with value μk\mu_{k} and size mj​km_{jk} in dimension jj, to maximize the total value while fitting into a knapsack with capacity DjD_{j} in dimension jj, where μk\mu_{k} and DjD_{j} are positive integers and mj​km_{jk} is a nonnegative integer.

We construct a corresponding instance of our problem: each item kk corresponds to a feasible server chain with service rate μk\mu_{k}; each dimension jj corresponds to a server with M~j=Dj\widetilde{M}_{j}=D_{j} cache slots after block placement; each server j∈[d]j\in[d] hosts mj:=maxk∈[K]⁡mj​km_{j}:=\max_{k\in[K]}m_{jk} blocks {1+∑j′=1j−1mj′,…,∑j′=1jmj′}\{1+\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{j-1}m_{j^{\prime}},\ldots,\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{j}m_{j^{\prime}}\}; the total number of blocks is L:=1+∑j∈[d]mjL:=1+\sum_{j\in[d]}m_{j}. In addition, for each k∈[K]k\in[K] and each j∈[d]j\in[d] with mj​k<mjm_{jk}<m_{j}, add a server vj​kv_{jk} before jj onto chain kk that hosts the same first mj−mj​km_{j}-m_{jk} blocks as jj with mj−mj​km_{j}-m_{jk} cache slots; for each chain k∈[K]k\in[K], add a server at the end that hosts the last block with 11 cache slot. By the above construction, we have KK server chains that can each run up to one job at a time, and enabling chain kk to run a job requires mj​km_{jk} cache slots at server j∈[d]j\in[d]. Thus, the decision version of MKP “is there a feasible solution to (32) with objective value ≥μ\geq\mu?” is equivalent to the feasibility test of the constructed subproblem of (7) with the KK constructed server chains and λ/ρ¯:=μ\lambda/\overline{\rho}:=\mu. As the decision version of MKP is NP-complete [15], the subproblem of (7) is NP-hard. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.2.

Since ∑j∈𝒥kmj​(c)≥L\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}m_{j}(c)\geq L, we can place the entire set of blocks onto each subset of servers 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} (∀k∈𝒦\forall k\in\mathcal{K}). Let kk denote the chain corresponding to 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k}. Each chain kk has a mean service time no greater than ∑j∈𝒥ktj​(c)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}t_{j}(c), as the mean time spent at each j∈𝒥kj\in\mathcal{J}_{k} is upper-bounded by tj​(c)t_{j}(c). The service rate of chain kk is thus no less than (∑j∈𝒥ktj​(c))−1(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}t_{j}(c))^{-1}. Moreover, according to (8), this block placement leaves enough residual memory at each server to process cc jobs concurrently. This completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

We prove the claim via a reduction from the partition problem [11]. Given a set of positive integers 𝒳:={x1,…,xN}\mathcal{X}:=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\} where NN is an even number, the partition problem determines if there exists a partition of 𝒳\mathcal{X} into two subsets 𝒳1,𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2} with equal sum. We construct a corresponding instance of our problem (10) by: (i) constructing a server jj for each number xjx_{j} with mj​(c)=tj​(c)=xjm_{j}(c)=t_{j}(c)=x_{j}, and (ii) setting L:=(∑j=1Nxj)/2L:=(\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_{j})/2 and λ/(ρ¯​c):=2/L\lambda/(\overline{\rho}c):=2/L. If there is no feasible solution to the partition problem, then the constructed problem has only one server group 𝒥′⊆[N]\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\subseteq[N] that satisfies (10c), with a scaled total service rate of

1∑j∈𝒥′xj≤1L,\displaystyle{1\over\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}x_{j}}\leq{1\over L}, (33)

which cannot satisfy the constraint (10b). If there is a feasible solution (𝒳1,𝒳2)(\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2}) to the partition problem, then (𝒥1,𝒥2)(\mathcal{J}_{1},\mathcal{J}_{2}) with 𝒥k:={j:xj∈𝒳k}\mathcal{J}_{k}:=\{j:\>x_{j}\in\mathcal{X}_{k}\} is a feasible solution to (10). Thus, testing the feasibility of the constructed instance of (10) will solve the partition problem. Since the partition problem is NP-complete [11], (10) is NP-hard. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.4.

Since Mj≡MM_{j}\equiv M, mj​(c)≡m​(c)m_{j}(c)\equiv m(c), and constraint (10c) reduces to |𝒥k|≥⌈L/m⁡(c)⌉=:n⁡(c)|\mathcal{J}_{k}|\geq\lceil L/m(c)\rceil=:n(c). Let (𝒥k∗)k∈𝒦∗(\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k})_{k\in\mathcal{K}^{*}} be an optimal solution to (10). Without loss of generality, we assume that Tk1:=∑j∈𝒥k1∗tj​(c)≤∑j∈𝒥k2∗tj​(c)=:Tk2T_{k_{1}}:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{1}}}t_{j}(c)\leq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{2}}}t_{j}(c)=:T_{k_{2}} for any k1<k2k_{1}<k_{2} (interpreted as “chain k1k_{1} is constructed before chain k2k_{2}”), and |𝒥k∗|≡n⁡(c)|\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k}|\equiv n(c) (∀k∈𝒦∗\forall k\in\mathcal{K}^{*}). Suppose that ∃k1<k2\exists k_{1}<k_{2} and j1∈𝒥k1∗,j2∈𝒥k2∗j_{1}\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{1}},\>j_{2}\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{2}} such that tj1​(c)>tj2​(c)t_{j_{1}}(c)>t_{j_{2}}(c). Then

1Tk1−tj1​(c)+tj2​(t)+1Tk2−tj2​(c)+tj1​(c)−1Tk1−1Tk2\displaystyle{1\over T_{k_{1}}-t_{j_{1}}(c)+t_{j_{2}}(t)}+{1\over T_{k_{2}}-t_{j_{2}}(c)+t_{j_{1}}(c)}-{1\over T_{k_{1}}}-{1\over T_{k_{2}}}
=\displaystyle= tj1​(c)−tj2​(c)(Tk1−tj1​(c)+tj2​(c))​Tk1−tj1​(c)−tj2​(c)(Tk2+tj1​(c)−tj2​(c))​Tk2>0,\displaystyle{t_{j_{1}}(c)-t_{j_{2}}(c)\over(T_{k_{1}}-t_{j_{1}}(c)+t_{j_{2}}(c))T_{k_{1}}}-{t_{j_{1}}(c)-t_{j_{2}}(c)\over(T_{k_{2}}+t_{j_{1}}(c)-t_{j_{2}}(c))T_{k_{2}}}>0, (34)

i.e., swapping j1j_{1} and j2j_{2} can only increase the scaled total service rate and thus the resulting solution remains optimal. Thus, there must exist an optimal solution to (10) in which tj1​(c)≤tj2​(c)t_{j_{1}}(c)\leq t_{j_{2}}(c) for all k1<k2k_{1}<k_{2} and j1∈𝒥k1∗,j2∈𝒥k2∗j_{1}\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{1}},\>j_{2}\in\mathcal{J}^{*}_{k_{2}}. Moreover, it must be optimal to use the fastest |𝒦∗||\mathcal{K}^{*}| chains. Therefore, an optimal solution to (10) is to group servers into server chains in the increasing order of tj​(c)t_{j}(c) until the scaled total service rate satisfies the requirement, which is exactly what is done in GBP-CR since t~j​(c)∝tj​(c)\widetilde{t}_{j}(c)\propto t_{j}(c) in this case. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.5.

First, suppose that when JFFS assigns a job at time tt, the fastest chain in 𝒦\mathcal{K} with available capacity according to 𝒄\bm{c} is klk_{l}. Then all the faster chains k1,…,kl−1k_{1},\ldots,k_{l-1} in 𝒦\mathcal{K} must be fully occupied at this time, i.e., running ck1,…,ckl−1c_{k_{1}},\ldots,c_{k_{l-1}} jobs respectively. Thus, the set of feasible links ℰ⁡(t):={(i,j)∈ℰ𝒂,𝒎:j​ has at least ​mi​j​ available cache slots at time ​t}⊆ℰ(l−1)\mathcal{E}(t):=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\bm{a},\bm{m}}:\>j\mbox{ has at least }m_{ij}\mbox{ available cache slots at time }t\}\subseteq\mathcal{E}^{(l-1)}. This implies that the length of the shortest j0→jJ+1j_{0}\to j_{J+1} path in 𝒢⁡(t)=(𝒥+,ℰ⁡(t))\mathcal{G}(t)=(\mathcal{J}_{+},\mathcal{E}(t)) is no smaller than the length of the shortest j0→jJ+1j_{0}\to j_{J+1} path in 𝒢(l−1)=(𝒥+,ℰ(l−1))\mathcal{G}^{(l-1)}=(\mathcal{J}_{+},\mathcal{E}^{(l-1)}), i.e., chain klk_{l} achieves the minimum mean service time among all the server chains with available capacity at time tt, including those outside 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Therefore, it suffices for JFFS to always assign jobs to chains in 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

Moreover, when kl∈𝒦k_{l}\in\mathcal{K} is selected by JFFS for processing a job at time tt, every faster chain kl′k_{l^{\prime}} with l′<ll^{\prime}<l must be running ckl′c_{k_{l^{\prime}}} jobs, and thus the number of available cache slots Mj​(t)M_{j}(t) at this time on each server jj must be upper-bounded by Mj(l−1)M^{(l-1)}_{j}. This implies that the maximum number of jobs chain klk_{l} can run at time tt is no more than cklc_{k_{l}}. Thus, JFFS assigns no more than ckc_{k} jobs on each k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K} at any point in time. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.6.

First, it is easy to see that any state (n,𝒄1:K)(n,\bm{c}_{1:K}) in 𝒵2\mathcal{Z}_{2} communicates with the state (0,𝒄1:K)(0,\bm{c}_{1:K}) through arrivals and departures. Meanwhile, any state (0,𝒛1:K)(0,\bm{z}_{1:K}) in 𝒵1\mathcal{Z}_{1} can reach (0,𝒄1:K)(0,\bm{c}_{1:K}) through arrivals, and can also be reached from (0,𝒄1:K)(0,\bm{c}_{1:K}) through departures. Thus, (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} is irreducible.

Next, we use the Foster–Lyapunov Criterion to prove positive recurrence. Define a Lyapunov function V⁡(𝒛):=z0V(\bm{z}):=z_{0} and a finite set 𝒞:=𝒵1\mathcal{C}:=\mathcal{Z}_{1}. Then for any 𝒛∉𝒞\bm{z}\not\in\mathcal{C}, the Lyapunov drift satisfies

Δ​V​(𝒛):=∑𝒛′q⁡(𝒛,𝒛′)​(V⁡(𝒛′)−V⁡(𝒛))=λ−∑l=1Kcl​μl<0.\displaystyle\Delta V(\bm{z}):=\sum_{\bm{z}^{\prime}}q(\bm{z},\bm{z}^{\prime})(V(\bm{z}^{\prime})-V(\bm{z}))=\lambda-\sum_{l=1}^{K}c_{l}\mu_{l}<0. (35)

For any 𝒛∈𝒞\bm{z}\in\mathcal{C}, the Lyapunov drift satisfies Δ​V​(𝒛)≤λ\Delta V(\bm{z})\leq\lambda. Thus, by the Foster–Lyapunov Criterion, (𝒁⁡(t))t≥0(\bm{Z}(t))_{t\geq 0} is positive recurrent, which completes the proof. ∎
